analysis.title: Heavy Metal: A Deep Dive On The Nuclear Fuel Cycle (Ahead of the Curve)
key_insights: TD Cowen sees a constructive backdrop for uranium mining and conversion, driven by nuclear capacity growth, constrained supply and fuel-security concerns. Cameco and Denison Mines are the top uranium picks.

Long-term uranium price forecast raised to $100/lb from $95/lb on October 22, 2026. A real price of $100/lb from 2030 is the level the firm says is needed to fund new mines and cover permitting and execution risk.

Spot uranium moved higher in two stages since October 2025. The first leg went to about $82/lb after Cameco cut McArthur River guidance and Kazatomprom lowered its 2026 outlook. The second leg reached the high $80s by mid-2026 and a spike to $100/lb in early 2026, helped by physical fund purchases.

Term uranium price rose modestly to $96/lb, about 12% YTD, and is at a record. Term contracting volume was 42.2Mlbs across 32 transactions as of September 28, slightly below 2022-2025 levels. The 35.5Mlb jump in early October mostly reflects booking of previously awarded volumes.
Utilities are contracting below replacement levels and feel sticker shock on pricing. TD Cowen expects uncovered requirements to force larger purchases later this decade and into the 2030s.
The WNA counts about 441 operable reactors (404 GW), 80 reactors (87 GW) under construction and 123 reactors (112 GW) planned. China has 38 units under construction and 43 planned.

Each operating GW needs about 0.4-0.5Mlbs U3O8 a year for reloads, and new reactors need about 1.5Mlbs/GW for initial cores. A 50GW AP1000 build-out by 2040 needs about 70Mlbs for initial cores plus 20+Mlbs a year afterward.

TD Cowen's supply/demand model has a deficit of 4-6Mlbs a year in 2026-2028, a surplus of 1-20Mlbs in 2030-2033, and a deficit of 19Mlbs in 2034 and 61Mlbs in 2035 as world mine supply falls 8.4% y/y in 2035.

TD Cowen's 2025 weighted average uranium cash cost is $21.65/lb across 29 operations covering about 97% of global supply. ISR averages about $19/lb and conventional about $25/lb. AISC is $31-35/lb before royalties and taxes.

Kazatomprom produced 13,291tU in H1/26, up 9% y/y, and held 2026 guidance of 27,500-29,000tU. Cameco kept attributable 2026 guidance of 19.5-21.5Mlbs, and H1/26 Canadian output fell 5% y/y to 10.1Mlbs.
The US ban on Russian low-enriched uranium has waivers expiring at the end of 2027, with a hard cutoff from January 1, 2028. This supports contracting urgency in conversion, enrichment and uranium.
In June 2026 the US DOE issued a conditional commitment for US$17.5bln of loans for long-lead equipment for up to ten AP1000 reactors across five sites, about 11 GW.

Global conversion demand is projected to rise from about 66,000tU in 2026 to 82,500tU by 2030 and 145,000-200,000tU by 2040, against licensed primary capacity of about 70,000tU. The firm expects deficits later this decade unless new capacity is added.
Secondary conversion supply is expected to fall from about 7,500tU in 2026 to 1,500-2,500tU by 2035. Conversion is about 5% of total fuel cost, and capacity utilization was about 91% in 2024.

Enrichment capacity was 64.5MM SWU against demand of 54.0MM SWU in 2025, with Russia's Rosatom holding 43% of capacity. Enrichment prices rose about 4x from about $50/SWU to about $200/SWU, and the long-term price is $181/SWU.

TD Cowen counts 14.2MM SWU of planned or under-construction western gaseous centrifuge capacity, about 60% of existing regional capacity. A further 11.5MM SWU is planned by laser enrichers GLE and LIS Technologies. Whether the market ends up over- or undersupplied is unclear.
Enrichment capex benchmarks are about $1,400/SWU for Orano's Project IKE and about $1,430/SWU for Urenco's Eunice expansion. Centrus is expected at $1,700-3,100/SWU ($6-11B for 3.5MM SWU).
Illustrative payback on new SWU capacity at $181/SWU is 7.8-15.6 years for Urenco/Orano-type costs and 14.6-26.8 years for Centrus, which TD Cowen calls seemingly unattractive.
Enrichment is a small part of reactor fuel cost. At $181/SWU it is about $3.20/MWh, and each $10/SWU change moves cost by $0.178/MWh. Raising the price to $250/SWU adds $1.24/MWh to an AP1000.

DOE issued first major enrichment task orders in January 2026: $900MM each to Centrus and General Matter for HALEU and to Orano for LEU. Centrus finalized its HALEU task order in July 2026 and must deliver 1 MTU of HALEU by July 2032.

Recycling conventional light water fuel is economic only if uranium prices rise about 4-6x, to $355-575/lb for light-water-to-light-water recycling. Recycling fast reactor fuel in fast reactors could have fuel costs below fresh uranium, but it needs a fleet of fast reactors that does not exist.
Recycled fast reactor fuel costs $3,902-8,100/kg against fresh HALEU at about $28,000/kg in TD Cowen's illustration. Recycled light water fuel for fast reactors is $24,569-56,875/kg.

Centrus was initiated at Hold with a $120 price target on uncertainty over enrichment returns. Oklo was initiated at Hold with a $26 price target on uncertainty over reactor and recycling costs. X-energy is the preferred pure-play reactor technology company and GE Vernova has the most commercial progress among public reactor designs.

market_movers.rationale: Top uranium pick. Vertically integrated with Tier-1 mines, a leading role in conversion, and a 49% stake in Global Laser Enrichment.
Top SMID-cap pick. Phoenix at Wheeler River is targeted for first production by mid-2028 as Canada's first commercial-scale ISR uranium mine.

Moved from developer to producer with Christensen Ranch and Burke Hollow. TD Cowen sees a path to 5Mlbs by the end of the decade. Its proposed UR&C conversion facility is not expected to produce this decade.
Arrow is under construction with completion targeted for H2/2030 and 30Mlbs U3O8 at full production. TD Cowen thinks NexGen could attract M&A interest.
TD Cowen expects a re-rate as IsoEnergy executes exploration across its Athabasca portfolio, including the Hurricane deposit.

Only public pure-play enrichment company with established technology pursuing expansion. Returns are uncertain given first-of-a-kind capex of about $1,700-3,100/SWU and payback of about 15-27 years at current SWU prices.
Only public company developing a sodium fast reactor with pyroprocessing recycling, which could be highly disruptive if it works. Recycling costs are unproven.
TD Cowen sees GE Vernova as having the most commercial progress among public company reactor designs.

sector_views.rationale: Structurally tight market through the balance of the decade with a higher long-term price needed to build new mines.
Balanced for the next few years, with deficits expected later this decade as secondary supply falls and demand rises.
Currently tight, but about 14.2MM SWU of western capacity plans, high capex and state-owned competition create uncertainty around returns.
Light water recycling is uneconomic without much higher uranium prices. Fast reactor closed-loop recycling could be viable but needs a fast reactor fleet.

risk_factors: Reactor delays and a faster-than-expected supply ramp are the principal downside risks to the uranium price view.
Planned enrichment additions, high capital costs and state-owned competition could challenge enrichment returns.
Utilities may keep contracting below replacement levels, delaying a full contracting cycle.
Recycling processing costs are unproven, and weapons proliferation concerns are a barrier.
Regulatory delays or rejections of nuclear module designs, or any malfunction at the world's nuclear assets, would hurt nuclear stocks.
Mining projects face technical, permitting, political, financial and environmental risks.
charts_described: Figure 1 plots the uranium spot price from August 2025 to August 2026 with annotated events: KAP reduced 2026 guidance, CCO cut McArthur River guidance by 3-4Mlbs, and SPUT purchases through Sep-Nov.
Figure 3 sets out TD Cowen's supply/demand model with a Supply/Demand Balance of -14 Mlb in 2023, -9 in 2024, 0 in 2025, -6 in 2026, 1 in 2030, 20 in 2031, and -61 in 2035.
Figure 37 shows Urenco cost per SWU capacity rising from $35 in 2019 to $85 in 2025, and EBITDA margin falling from 68% to 38%.
geopolitical: US ban on Russian low-enriched uranium has waivers expiring at the end of 2027, with a hard cutoff from January 1, 2028.
Russia accounts for 43% of global enrichment capacity and is being prohibited in several markets after its invasion of Ukraine.
Russia restricted exports of Russian LEU to the US in response to the 2024 Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act.
TD Cowen notes that an end to the Russia/Ukraine conflict would not automatically let Russian volume into the US after 2027, because the Act is a statute that needs legal or legislative action.

tension_points.bull_case: Russia is 43% of global capacity and the US ban takes effect in 2028. Demand from restarts, uprates and new builds is rising. Enrichment prices are up about 4x to about $200/SWU. TD Cowen estimates planned additions leave about 9MM SWU for new reactors, enough for more than 60GW.
tension_points.bear_case: About 14.2MM SWU of western capacity is planned, equal to about 60% of regional capacity, with another 11.5MM SWU planned by laser enrichers. Capex of about $1,400-3,100/SWU implies paybacks of about 8-27 years at $181/SWU, and state-owned enterprises dominate the competition.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A larger share of announced capacity actually getting built and fewer retirements than expected would push the market toward oversupply.

tension_points.bull_case: Recycling fast reactor fuel in fast reactors could cost about $3,902-8,100/kg against about $28,000/kg for fresh HALEU. Nuclear capacity aspirations may strain fuel supply and support recycling.
tension_points.bear_case: Light water recycling is inefficient and needs uranium at about $355-575/lb. Fast reactor recycling needs a fast reactor fleet that does not exist, and processing costs are unproven.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Light water recycling stays uneconomic unless uranium reaches about $355/lb at the low end, assuming flat SWU prices.

tension_points.bull_case: Utilities are contracting below replacement levels, uncovered requirements are building, and the Russian LEU ban and diversified supply needs support contracting later this decade.
tension_points.bear_case: Utilities are feeling sticker shock and are reluctant to contract, term volume of 42.2Mlbs is below 2022-2025 levels, and near-term coverage tempers urgency.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sustained period of contracting below replacement levels that does not recover would undercut the structural tightness view.
